title: Circuit, Packet Switching & Network Delay
summary: See how data actually moves through a network — circuit vs packet switching — and learn the four delay components engineers reason about when something feels slow.

slides.sectionTitle: How data moves through a network
slides.markdown: Two fundamentally different ways exist to move data across a shared network: reserve a dedicated path for the whole conversation (**circuit switching**), or chop data into independent chunks that share the network opportunistically (**packet switching**). The internet chose the second, and every delay you experience online is one of four specific components — not a vague "it's slow."

**Circuit switching** reserves a dedicated, fixed-capacity path between two endpoints for the entire duration of a session — the classic example is the old telephone network, where a call physically reserved a line through the exchange.

Once reserved, that capacity is yours alone, guaranteed and unshared, whether you're talking or sitting in silence. That guarantee is also the downside: idle time on a reserved circuit is capacity nobody else can use, even during a lull in conversation.

**Packet switching** breaks data into independent packets, each carrying its own destination address, and forwards them **store-and-forward**: a router receives a whole packet, checks it, then sends it on. No path is reserved in advance.

Multiple conversations share the same link via **statistical multiplexing** — betting that not everyone transmits at once, so idle capacity from one flow gets used by another. This is why the internet scales far more cheaply than a dedicated-circuit network ever could, at the cost of no hard capacity guarantee per flow.

| | Circuit switching | Packet switching |
|---|---|---|
| Capacity | Dedicated, guaranteed | Shared, best-effort |
| Efficiency | Wastes idle time | High — statistical multiplexing |
| Latency | Fixed, predictable once set up | Variable — depends on load |
| Failure handling | One link failure kills the call | Packets can reroute around a failure |

**How to decide:** circuit switching wins when you need a hard latency/capacity guarantee (legacy telephony); packet switching wins whenever efficiency and resilience to failure matter more than a guarantee — which is nearly everything today.

Every packet's end-to-end delay is the sum of four components at every hop:

- **Propagation delay** — time for the signal to physically travel the wire/fiber/air (distance ÷ speed of transmission).
- **Transmission delay** — time to push all the packet's bits onto the link (packet size ÷ link rate).
- **Queuing delay** — time waiting in a router's buffer behind other packets.
- **Processing delay** — time for the router to inspect the header and decide where to send it.

Only queuing delay is genuinely unpredictable — the other three are near-constant for a given path and packet size.

Delay accumulates at every hop, not just once end-to-end:

![A packet's delay breakdown hop by hop across three routers](assets/packet-delay-breakdown.svg)

A "slow" connection is often one overloaded router adding queuing delay at a single hop — not a uniformly slow path.

slides.markdown:
The **bandwidth-delay product** (bandwidth × round-trip time) tells you how many bits can be "in flight" on the link at once — effectively the pipe's volume, not just its width.

A high-bandwidth, high-latency link (e.g. satellite) can have a huge bandwidth-delay product: you need a large amount of unacknowledged data in flight to actually fill that pipe, which is exactly why TCP's window-sizing (covered in the transport layer) matters so much for long-haul or satellite links.

slides.subTitle: "I upgraded to gigabit and my game still lags"
slides.markdown:
A common mistake: upgrading **bandwidth** (capacity, bits/second) expecting it to fix **latency** (delay, time for one bit to arrive) — they measure different things. A gigabit connection with a satellite uplink can still have 600ms round-trip latency; a modest DSL line to a nearby server can feel snappier for interactive traffic.

Bandwidth helps when you're moving large volumes (downloads, streaming); latency dominates when you're doing small, frequent round-trips (gaming, video calls, page-load waterfalls). Diagnose which one you actually have before "upgrading."
